description: We are five engineers who are determined to develop solutions for biomedical challenges in hard environments like space. We are interested in simplifying systems to facilitate life activities.
summary: RCPT (Radiation-Coupled Physiological Twin) is an offline health-monitoring app for astronauts on Moon and Mars missions. Messages between Mars and Earth can take up to about 20 minutes each way, so a crew cannot always wait for doctors on the ground. Space radiation, lost sleep and heart-rate strain also make each other worse, and this is hard to judge by eye. RCPT combines these three signals into one live risk score from 0 to 100 with three levels: nominal, elevated and emergency. It then suggests an action, such as a rest or shelter protocol. Every number can be opened and explained, and every value is labelled as simulated, derived or not modeled. It also shows a body view by organ system, gives rule-based cues from eye and skin photos, and includes an offline assistant called Nova in English, Arabic and Spanish. It matters because crews far from Earth need clear, trustworthy health information that works without a connection. This is a research prototype that uses simulated data. It is not a medical device.
details:
Our project pairs three lightweight wearable sensor nodes with an offline software “physiological twin” that runs entirely inside the spacecraft. It turns raw body signals, radiation exposure and sleep debt into one clear risk score, explains how that score was reached, and shows which part of the body is under the most strain. No Earth link is needed to detect, understand or react to a developing medical problem.

The Problem

On a Mars mission, Earth is too far to be a first responder. A signal takes up to 22 minutes to arrive, so a call for help and a reply can take 44 minutes or more. For a cardiac event, a radiation-driven crisis or a sudden neurological problem, that gap can decide the outcome.

Moreover, astronauts are expected to run a mission and also act as their own doctors. In a cramped habitat, with altered gravity, fatigue and a heavy workload, they cannot reliably or regularly assess their own condition, even when diagnostic equipment is on board.

So the real need is not more medical equipment. It is continuous, automatic, local health awareness that asks nothing of the crew.

Our Solution

We built a two-part system:

•     Hardware: a tri-node wearable network (head, chest, wrist) that measures continuously and is always ready on the body.

•     Software (RCPT): an offline web application that fuses those signals with radiation and sleep data, scores crew risk in real time, and explains every number.

Everything runs locally on the ship. Nothing depends on the signal to Earth.

How the System Works

Step 1. Sense. Head and chest nodes capture microvolt-level brain (EEG) and heart (ECG) signals and clean them locally.

Step 2. Aggregate. They send compact data packets over Bluetooth Low Energy to the wrist hub, which adds blood pressure, oxygen saturation and in-suit environment readings.

Step 3. Transmit. The wrist hub sends one synchronized telemetry packet through the suit by RF link to the habitat’s local server.

Step 4. Understand. RCPT software combines the telemetry with radiation dose and sleep debt and computes a live risk index from 0 to 100.

Step 5. Act. The crew sees the score, the affected organ systems and a plain-language explanation, by screen or by voice, and gets the right alert tier: nominal, elevated or emergency.

Hardware: The Tri-Node Wearable System

Instead of one bulky device, we spread the sensing across three small nodes. Each sits where its signal is strongest, so no single piece is heavy, restrictive or awkward during work or sleep.

Why this design works

•     Edge processing first. Head and chest nodes filter and digitize their own signals, so only clean, compact data travels. That saves power and bandwidth.

•     One hub, one link. Only the wrist hub talks to the habitat, which keeps the wireless footprint small and the data synchronized.

•     Always ready. The nodes are worn continuously, so the system already has a baseline when an emergency begins.

Built for the Martian environment

•     Radiation hardening: silicon-on-insulator microcontrollers and error-correcting memory protect against bit-flips from cosmic rays.

•     Thermal control: electronics are encapsulated in thermally conductive, electrically insulating epoxy that passes

heat into the suit’s liquid cooling garment.

•     Dust protection: sealed housings (IP69K-equivalent) with PTFE membranes keep out abrasive, electrostatically charged regolith.

•     Low-gravity securement: elastomeric tensioners and micro-boa dials hold electrodes against the skin. Capacitive sensors track skin contact and warn the wearer if a node loses it.

Software: RCPT

•     Live risk index (0–100). Merges radiation dose, HRV and sleep debt into a single number.

•     Interaction model. These stressors compound instead of simply adding up, so a tired crew is hit harder by the same radiation.

•     Offline edge engine. All calculations stay on the device, so the app works with no connection at all.

•     Scenario buttons. Jump between calm orbit, a sleep-deprived crew and an acute solar storm. One click shows how the whole system reacts.

•     40-hour telemetry simulation. Shows risk climbing over time and tiers shifting from nominal to elevated to emergency.

•     Crew avatar. Breaks the overall score into organ systems so the most strained part of the body is visible.

•     Crew Quarters. Shows a sleeping astronaut and their organs in one scene, making sleep and recovery part of the picture.

•     Image assessment. Reads a photo of the eye or skin and returns color and pupil cues. It is rule-based and states clearly that it is not a diagnosis.

Validity

•     “How it is computed” panels. Every number can be opened and explained. Nothing is a black box.

•     Honest labelling. Each value is tagged simulated, derived or not modeled, so a simulation is never mistaken for a measurement.

•     Data and Validation area. The validation tab compares our radiation model with published Curiosity rover results and admits where it falls short. The sensitivity tab shows which assumptions move the result most. The sources tab lists every reference.

AI Assistant

•     NOVA AI is a chatbot available to answer questions through text or voice.

Simulated guided tutorials

•     Mars atlas and terrain tools. Place dose and conditions at real locations so mission planners can compare sites.

•     Guided tour and three languages. Anyone can open it, learn it and test the claims for themselves.

What Is Real and What Is Simulated

•     In our demo, we don’t have actual hardware, so sensor inputs are simulated from three parameters: sleep debt, radiation exposure and mission time.

•     In a flight version, the same inputs would come live from the tri-node hardware and crew dosimetry.

•     Outputs are decision support, not diagnosis. RCPT flags risk and explains it. It does not replace medical judgment.

Conclusion

The difference our solution makes is that health awareness moves from Earth to the crew itself. Instead of waiting 44 minutes for an answer, astronauts get a continuous, explainable picture of their own condition, built from light-weight wearable sensors and software that never needs a signal home. It is simple enough to use under stress, and stand by to act in emergencies.
